chapter: Corrections and views on early Black music
title: Wendell McNeil and John Robichaux's orchestras in New Orleans
summary: White recalls playing trumpet for Wendell McNeil's society band, the engagements and dress code, and John Robichaux's playing.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Now those things should be contradicted and should be roundly contradicted. Should be openly denounced. You want to discredit people who actually put, what are you going to do about James Rodden Johnson and Jay Rosamund Johnson who come along before any of us? Now Jay Rosamund is still alive. If he hasn't died lately. I don't think so. And a more qualified composer and an exponent of the piano you never heard in his boyhood days. His home is Jacksonville, Florida. Wendell McNeil, John McNeil, they came along ahead of Manuel's time. Oh yeah. But those fellas served as fine musicians in the Spanish-American War. And I played with Wendell. I was Wendell's trumpet player. And if Wendell didn't get me, the engagement went come from him. Because he didn't go, he didn't go look for anybody else. You had to read Wendell's scores just like that. Now Will said that he had the second Robichaux orchestra. Robichaux's main officer was in the Lyric Theater. But when Robichaux leave the orchestra, he'd come where Wendell was playing because it was his engagement. Robichaux was one of the well-known men in New Orleans, you see. So he could get these high type engagements at Antwine, at the, in the Gold Room of the Sonnyak Club. And all those places. The Roosevelt Hotel. And the, on the, what's that other big hotel there? St. Charles. St. Charles. We played in the St. Charles, too. We played in every hole there was in the St. Charles. We played in Antwine down there so many times, all them TU ducks. They used to give us half TU ducks. When Wendell's band's sitting there, your tie was speak and span. You didn't pull off a coat to play in there. Like the glue of the dance hall. The guys come in the dance hall, they just took off his coat and open up his shirt. I said, what are you going to do, fight? Well, Wendell's band's sitting there, your tie was speak and span. You had to be well-groomed. Your shoes shine. You look speak and span. And your coat buttoned as you walked through if you haven't got on your vest. And your full dress is there like anybody else. And we, a Wendell's officer, when services handed around, our service was handed right there, too, the same way. Now, that's the way New Orleans was when I was down there. And I love New Orleans. And I made no more money in New Orleans than I ever made in any place in my life. You got to cut off at you? No.
No, no, no, you're not saying anything out of the way. Oh, oh, all right.
Unless you do want to cut it off or anything. No, no, that's all right. But I'm telling you.
You're not talking about anybody except to say something good about the old music. He said a little bit about Duke, but he needs to be straight.

Yeah, he should be criticized. He should be. But as for John Robichaux's officers down there, the officers that John sent out under Wendell McNeil. Wendell was his conductor until he come on the scene. And when John come on the scene, John is king. And John take over that left-hand fiddle and start playing. And the people stop John. Hey, John, come here.

Wealthy people. New Orleans is loaded with a massive wealth. You know that, don't you? The Sugar Kings, the Cotton Kings, all that Dean Witter and company down there. John had to quit playing with his body on his arm, so he's walking around the floor, you see, and something once around there. But he's a celebrity like anybody else. That was John Robichaux. Mary Robinson played every duck there was on that sheet. Not a duck missing. Wendell on his violin, equally as good. And he could play some violin too. A man would tell you. He could play a French horn and he could play violin. But he was carrying the mail, you know. And he was a fine fellow, so jokish, so lovable, so sweet to talk with. Well, see, if you make a little mistake, you can't have it.
I said, but look at what we're good now. I said, are we going to play that?

All new music. They open it out in the batches right there. And you played it. Now, if he had a repertoire of that, if we played it before by request, he'd have it there. And old John was deaf on his music. Now, you wouldn't know whether John was playing his right or not, because he played left, and you could hear the things all kind of hours.
But when you could know manners.
